name: Jyotisha and Panchangam in Kerala
tagline: How Kerala reads time, festivals and auspicious moments
summary: Kerala's jyotisha (traditional astrology) and the panchangam (almanac) combine sidereal astronomy and local rules to fix tithis, nakshatras, muhurta and festival dates used across the state.
description: Jyotisha is the classical Indian system of astronomy-astrology; in Kerala it is used practically through the panchangam (panjika) — the day-by-day almanac that lists tithi, nakshatra, yoga, karana and vara plus sunrise, muhurta and inauspicious windows.

Kerala follows the Kollam era (Kollavarsham) — a sidereal solar reckoning whose year begins on Chingam 1 (mid‑August) — while many festival and ritual dates depend on the panchangam's lunar tithi and nakshatra readings.

Panchangams in Kerala appear as printed panjika books and as modern digital services; they are used to choose wedding muhurths, temple rites, ancestral tarpan, festival dates (Onam, Vishu, Karkidaka Vavu, Thrissur Pooram) and daily temple timings.

Visitors get a window into Kerala’s calendar culture: reading festival timing, watching temple offices and priests consult the panchangam, buying local panjika booklets or checking location‑specific online panchang tools.
highlights: The five limbs: tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga and karana
Kerala uses the Kollam era (Kollavarsham) — a sidereal solar calendar
Local rule differences (e.g., aparahna rule) sometimes shift Malayalam month starts
Panchangam guides festival dates, muhurta, Rahu-Kaal and other daily windows
Available as traditional printed panjika and modern apps/web panchangams

sections.heading: Background
body: Jyotisha in Kerala is the practical marriage of sidereal astronomy and ritual practice. The panchangam is the everyday output: a daily sheet or page listing the five limbs (tithi, vara, nakshatra, yoga, karana), sunrise/sunset and time-windows used for auspicious or avoided actions.

Kerala’s civil and temple dates normally use the Kollam era (Kollavarsham), a sidereal solar calendar that scholars date to 825 CE; local traditions and historical accounts give several origin stories, presented as tradition rather than fact.

sections.heading: How the panchangam is made (brief)
body: Modern panchangams compute planetary and lunar longitudes from astronomical ephemerides, convert tropical to sidereal positions (Lahiri ayanamsa is common) and derive tithis (12° steps of Moon–Sun longitude), nakshatras (27 × 13°20′ divisions) and karanas (half‑tithis).

Regional rules matter: Kerala almanacs apply the aparahna rule and certain temple conventions when fixing the day for a festival or month start; different publishers (vakya/traditional versus drik/astronomical) may show small timing differences, so people often check the edition used by a temple or family.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Buy or browse a local panjika (booklet) at bookstores and temple offices; newspapers and major Kerala publishers print annual panjika editions. Online, Kerala-rooted services and national digital panchangams provide city-specific daily panchang data and muhurta calculators.

Visit temple offices or major temple festivals to see the panchangam in use: priests, tantris and temple administrators consult the almanac for ritual timing. You can also ask at a temple office for the printed panjika or a recommended local jyotishi (astrologer) — always observe temple etiquette.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: If you travel to Kerala for a festival or ritual, confirm the date with the temple or organiser in advance — different almanac traditions can shift a date by hours. For personal muhurta planning bring exact birth data (date, time, place) and consult a recognized astrologer if you need formal chart work.

Use location-specific panchang tools (choose the city or coordinates) rather than a generic national table: sunrise-based tithi (udaya tithi) and regional conventions determine the right day for many observances in Kerala.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Year-round; check the panchangam for specific festival dates (Onam, Vishu, Karkidaka Vavu, Thrissur Pooram) before you travel.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Panchangam information and printed panjika are available across Kerala — find them in temple offices, local bookstores and newspaper stalls; major digital panchang services let you choose any Kerala city for location‑specific timings.
etiquette: Always confirm festival dates and muhurta with the temple or panjika publisher you plan to follow — local rules can change the date.
When asking for astrological help, bring exact birth time and birthplace; be respectful and clear about fees before the consultation.
At temples, follow local dress and behaviour codes when accompanying priests or viewing rituals scheduled by the panchangam.
